1.pericope_label: Forty years under the Philistines, and an angel to a barren woman

schools.summary: Gill glosses the evil as idolatry, the sin Israel was prone to and often guilty of.

Henry states the theology of the recurring formula in a line: had there been no sin there would have needed no Saviour, but sin was suffered to abound that grace might much more abound. He measures the oppressors and finds them small — five lords with but five cities of note, an inconsiderable people beside Israel, yet as the staff in God's hand oppressive and vexatious, and this trouble longer than any yet. On the annunciation he is fullest. The tribe he thinks significant, Dan meaning a judge, so that dying Jacob's word probably looked to this man, and Dan's lot lay next the Philistine country, which made a Danite the fittest bridle upon them. The long barrenness he reads as design, many eminent men having been born of mothers long kept from the blessing, that the mercy might be the more acceptable — mercies long waited for often prove signal mercies. He follows Bishop Patrick in taking the messenger for the Lord himself, the Word who was to be the Messiah, since his name is called Wonderful; and he notes the message was sent not for Manoah's sake but for Israel's, and beyond that for the Messiah's, whose type this child was and whose birth likewise had to be foretold by an angel. Even the opening words are tender: the angel names her barrenness not to upbraid her but because she was perhaps then bemoaning herself as one written childless.

Clarke qualifies the servitude. It does not appear that from Shamgar until now the Philistines were in a condition to oppress Israel, or were permitted to; and even now they had not entirely subjected them, since a sort of commerce still went on — they vexed and made inroads without holding them in complete subjection.

Ellicott identifies the nation, mentioned so far only in passing and from this point a leading part: not Canaanites but foreign conquerors holding a district originally the Avim's, their name meaning emigrants, their Cretan connection inferred from the name Cherethites, and their stock — Semitic, Hamitic or Aryan — disputed. He also supplies the chronology, the forty years ending at Ebenezer and the ark having been taken and returned about twenty years before, so that Samson's acts fall in those twenty years and Eli died about the time Samson came of age. Keil sets the chapter in a wider frame: while Jephthah delivered the tribes east of Jordan, the Philistine pressure west of it continued unbroken and grew heavier after the war in Eli's last years — yet even then God did not leave himself without witness, Dagon falling before the ark with head and arms broken.

debates.question: How complete was the Philistine domination?

positions.position: not complete — commerce continued between the two peoples; they vexed Israel and raided without holding them in entire subjection
unbroken and worsening, culminating in the defeat and the loss of the ark in Eli’s last years

outliers.note: reads the barrenness itself as design, on the rule that mercies long waited for often prove signal mercies

themes: a small nation made a great scourge
why the deliverer was a Danite born of a barren woman

2.pericope_label: Zorah, the man of God, and the Nazarite charge

schools.summary: Gill places Zorah on the border of Judah and Dan, reports Josephus making Manoah a principal man of rank and figure where the Talmudists call him a plebeian, and notes the mother must drink neither new wine nor old, the reason appearing in the next verse. On the messenger he is emphatic: not a mere man, not a prophet, not even a created angel, but the uncreated Angel of the covenant, the Son and Word of God who often appeared in human form, since his name is Wonderful and he is called Jehovah.

Clarke says flatly that Zorah was a town of Judah afterwards given to Dan, and identifies the messenger as the same who appeared to Moses, to Joshua and to Gideon, no other than the second person of the Trinity. He agrees the mother must live the life of a Nazarite so long as she carried and nursed the child, and adds a textual note on her report: where the Hebrew has I asked him not whence he was, neither told he me his name, the Vulgate and part of the Greek tradition drop the negative, so that she asked and he would not tell her.

Ellicott notes the birth of Samuel is introduced almost the same way, and fills in the place — Zorah means place of hornets, identified by Robinson with Surah, whose conical hill and abundant fountain made it strong and convenient. He and Keil both observe that family and tribe are used interchangeably here, and explain it the same way: all the Danites made up the single family of Shuham. Ellicott finds meaning in the name Manoah, which signifies rest, sets the barren wife among Sarah, Rebekah, Hannah and Elizabeth, and remarks how many phrases here recur in the first chapter of Luke. On the vow he is precise: the mother takes on for a time part of the Nazarite obligation, strong drink meaning intoxicating liquor not made from grapes, and the law of clean and unclean, though binding on every Israelite, is pressed on her to impress the separated character of her son. He adds that when the law of the Nazarite in Numbers is read as the first lesson in the synagogue, this account of Samson, the first Nazarite on record, is read as the second — and reports a third opinion on the messenger, Rabbi Levi Ben Gershom's, that he was Phinehas, which he dismisses.

debates.question: Who was the man who appeared to Manoah's wife?

positions.position: the uncreated Angel of the covenant, the Son and Word of God
a supernatural being certainly, as in the appearances to Gideon and Zacharias — not, as one rabbi held, Phinehas

outliers.note: insists the woman herself took him for no more than a prophet, and notes Josephus turned him into a beautiful youth who roused Manoah's jealousy

themes: the mother’s share in the vow
why Samson would only begin the deliverance

8.pericope_label: Manoah's prayer, and the angel's second visit

schools.summary: Gill notes a liberty taken by Josephus, who makes the woman pray where the text is clear that Manoah did. He reads the clause now let thy words come to pass as not a wish merely but a prayer of faith, and observes that the angel returns no direct word either about what should be done to the child or what the child should do, but only repeats what he had said to the woman, which was enough for Manoah to know.

Henry defends Manoah before expounding him: he was not incredulous of his wife's story, knowing her a virtuous woman, still less was he — as Josephus unworthily represents him — jealous of her conversation with the stranger. What Henry finds in the prayer is faith of an unusual order, since Manoah speaks without hesitation of the child that shall be born; so great faith was not found, he says, no, not in Zechariah, a priest at the altar to whom the angel himself appeared. He weighs too what Manoah asks for, which is instruction rather than information: good men are more solicitous to know their duty than the events that will befall them, for duty is ours and events are God's. The manner pleases him as much — Manoah does not send servants abroad but seeks the man of God on his knees, and so seeking finds him. He draws lessons from the setting as well: solitude is often an opportunity for communion with God, good people having thought themselves never less alone than when alone; and the wife runs to fetch her husband rather than asking the messenger to come to him, since those who would meet with God must attend where he is pleased to manifest himself. His domestic moral is the warmest touch — to atone for the first fatal miscarriage, when Eve pressed Adam to what was evil, let yoke-fellows excite one another to good works, and no husband think it a disparagement to follow his wife in what is praiseworthy.
Clarke gives a plainer reason for the second visit: it was probably essential to Manoah's peace, who might else have been jealous, and now had proof the thing was of the Lord.

Keil renders Manoah's question closely — should thy word then come to pass, what will be the manner of the boy, and his doing? — and marks the single addition made this second time, the caution against eating anything of the vine, which brings the charge into line with the law of the Nazarite in Numbers. Ellicott gives the literal sense of the noun, what shall be the ordering of the child and his work, the word elsewhere meaning a right or a due; and sums up the visit shortly and probably rightly, that its object seems only to have been to give Manoah certainty.

debates.question: Why did the angel come a second time?

positions.position: to give Manoah certainty — the message itself adds almost nothing
for Manoah’s peace, who might otherwise have suspected his wife
because God will not fail to guide those who sincerely ask to know their duty

outliers.note: rates Manoah's faith above Zechariah's, and turns the wife's errand into a rule that husbands may follow their wives in what is praiseworthy

themes: a husband who believed his wife
asking for duty rather than for events
why the angel answered nothing new

15.pericope_label: A kid refused, and a name withheld

schools.summary: Gill has Manoah speak just as he sees the visitor means to say no more and is about to leave.

Henry takes the offered kid as gratitude and draws a rule — those who welcome the message will be kind to the messengers for the sake of him who sends them. The angel declines, as he had declined Gideon's, and turns the meal into an offering: angels need neither meat nor drink, the glorifying of God being their meat and drink as it was Christ's; and we do God's will in some measure as they do if we eat and drink to his glory, turning our common meals into sacrifices. That Manoah did not know whom he spoke to Henry counts a mercy, not an oversight, since had he known it the terror would have been such that he durst not have conversed at all — so Christ was in the world and the world knew him not, and we could not bear the sight of the divine glory unveiled. The refusal of the name he treats as the most instructive thing here. Manoah's motive was not doubt but honour, yet the request is denied: we have not what we ask when we ask we know not what. What he asked for the direction of his duty he was readily told; what he asked to gratify curiosity was refused, God having given full direction concerning our duty in his word but never designing to answer all the enquiries of a speculative head. The name is secret because the names of angels were not yet revealed, to prevent men idolizing them — after the captivity, when the church was cured of idolatry, angels named themselves to Daniel, and to Zacharias one gave his name unasked. But the word may equally be rendered wonderful, and one of Christ's names is Wonderful, long secret and brought to light by the gospel.
Clarke reads the offer simply: not knowing the man's quality, Manoah meant hospitality.

Ellicott finds the language genuinely ambiguous. The phrase is literally before thy face, the narrative runs parallel to the angel's appearance to Gideon, and the same uncertainty attaches to the terms, since the Hebrew verb, like the Greek and Latin answering to it, may mean either to do or to sacrifice — so we cannot decide whether a sacrifice or a meal was meant. He adds that a kid was a special delicacy.

debates.question: Did Manoah mean to offer a meal or a sacrifice?

positions.position: hospitality — he did not know the man’s quality
undecidable; the Hebrew verb, like the Greek and Latin, may mean either to do or to sacrifice

outliers.note: makes the refused name a rule about prayer: what is asked for the direction of duty is granted, what is asked to satisfy curiosity is not

themes: why the angel's nature was concealed

16.pericope_label: Wonderful: the sacrifice, the ascent, and the wife's reasoning

schools.summary: Gill has Manoah fetch the kid he meant for a meal and bring it as a burnt offering, joining a meat offering as was usual; and he observes that his wife was the less fearful and the stronger believer, comforting her husband with three arguments — that if the Lord had meant to kill them he would not have received their offering, nor shown them all these things, nor told them such things at such a time.

Clarke reads the angel's refusal as two in one: as a spiritual being he does not subsist by earthly food, and neither will he receive the homage belonging to God. On the name he turns the point evidentially — it was precisely because the name was secret that they wished to know it, but the angel does not say it is secret, he says it is Wonderful, the very character given to Jesus Christ by the prophet, so that some suppose he gives this as his name and was our blessed Lord. He ties the miracle to the name as well: he acted according to what he was called, and being wonderful did wonderful things, probably causing fire to rise from the rock and then ascending in the flame. Of the wife's argument he says it is excellent reasoning, and turns it into counsel for dark dispensations of providence — he who has preserved and borne with a man so long is not less willing to save him now, and the very light that shows a man his wretchedness proves God waiting to be gracious, the penitential pangs arguing a fire of God's kindling, sent to refine and not destroy.

Keil parses the question closely, since it reads literally who is thy name, the pronoun asking after a person rather than a nature, and the verb rendered do thee honour meaning to honour by presents. On the adjective he sets out the written and read forms and concludes it is not the angel's proper name but expresses the character of his name, and so the peculiarity of his nature: it is to be taken absolutely, supremely wonderful, a predicate belonging to God alone, and not toned down as Bertheau tones it. He explains why the rock is called an altar, the angel having sanctified it by the miraculous acceptance of the sacrifice. Ellicott presses the reproof of angel-worship, which the early Gnostic sects tended toward, but will not have the refusal of food pressed too far, since the angel might have partaken as the visitors to Abraham and Lot did — quoting Milton, that these pure intelligential substances require food as your rational does. On the adjective he holds a middle ground, that it is an adjective and not the actual name, adding the observation that settles it for him: the only angel who names himself anywhere in Scripture is Gabriel.

positions.position: quite possibly — it is the very title given to Christ by the prophet, and some take the angel to be our Lord
no — it is an adjective expressing the character of the name, taken absolutely and belonging to God alone

outliers.note: expands the wife's reasoning into pastoral counsel: the very light that shows a man his wretchedness proves God waiting to be gracious

themes: why the angel would not eat
whether Wonderful is the angel’s name
the wife’s three arguments against fear

24.pericope_label: Samson born, and the Spirit beginning to move him

schools.summary: Gill will not allow the name carries strength in it and takes it from the sun, offering three reasons why it might have been given — the splendour of the child's countenance at birth, the memory of the angel's shining countenance, or the darkness of the calamity he was to dispel. On the last verse he reads the Spirit as striking the boy's mind and impressing it with thoughts of great things to come, citing the Targum that the spirit of strength from the Lord began to strengthen him.

Henry takes the name as a type, deriving it from the word for sun turned into a diminutive — a little sun — because Samson, like Moses, was born to deliver and was exceedingly fair, and because if the sun may be compared to a strong man running his race, a strong man may as fairly be compared to the sun; he ends on Samson as a light to his people and a type of Christ the Sun of righteousness. On the growth he says the boy outgrew others of his age and more besides, so it appeared the Lord was fitting him for something extraordinary — children of promise shall have the blessing. His closing observation is the best in the chapter: the Spirit moved him at times, not at all times, but as the wind blows where it lists, which shows what he did was not from himself, for then he could have done it whenever he pleased. Strong men think themselves animated by wine, he adds, but Samson drank none and yet excelled in strength and courage, because the Spirit of God moved him — therefore be not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit.

Clarke traces the name to a root meaning to serve, making it either a little sun or a little servant, and prefers the second as just the name maternal fondness would impose on an only son. On the last verse he supplies the human side: Samson felt the degrading bondage of his countrymen and a desire to do something for their deliverance, and these feelings he had from the divine Spirit.

Ellicott reports Josephus rendering the name strong, and suspects he was not unwilling to hint an analogy with the Greek Hercules; Jerome made it strength of the sun; Ellicott himself thinks sunny likeliest, notes the rabbis said the boy was named after the name of God, who is called a sun and shield to Israel, and marks that here the mother gave the name. He cautions that the blessings alluded to appear to be health, strength and courage, and by no means set Samson on a level with Samuel or John the Baptist. On the closing verb he glosses it as to agitate or thrust, following Luther, implying vehement impulses to noble deeds which came on him only at times, and takes the Targum's spirit of courage from Jehovah as the right paraphrase. Keil rejects sun-like or hero of the sun and derives the name from a root meaning to be strong or daring; he renders the last verb as to thrust, an operation taking possession of Samson suddenly and impelling him to put forth supernatural powers, and notes with Ellicott that Mahaneh-dan and Eshtaol remain unidentified.

debates.question: What does the name Samson mean?

positions.position: strong or daring, from a root meaning to be powerful — so Josephus
from the sun: a little sun, or sunny, or the strength of the sun
from a root meaning to serve — a little servant, the name a fond mother would give an only son

outliers.note: checks the enthusiasm of the others, holding that health, strength and courage do not set Samson beside Samuel or John the Baptist

themes: a blessing of body rather than of grace
a Spirit that moved him only at times
